DWP says it has "taken some online services offline as a precaution" which implies that they have possibly seen some kind of activity on their IT network that doesn’t look right.
Taking services offline is part of a "Hail Mary" response we have seen in other cyber incidents, as it kicks the hackers out to prevent further intrusion. Cutting internet connectivity can also help responders preserve evidence, which might help if this is indeed some kind of malicious activity. But we also have to be wary of the language here, as DWP’s actions and wording are reminiscent of the Co-op hack last year.
In that incident Co-op said it had taken services offline as a "precaution". Only later did we discover that it was already too late, as the hackers had successfully breached the firm and stolen the data of 6.5 million customers. There is no suggestion at this stage that there has been a breach at DWP though - or even that the "cyber incident" is malicious.

### Systems like DWP are attractive targets to criminals - here's why published at 10:17 GMT

![Image 2](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/128/cpsprodpb//vivo/live/images/2022/9/26/0af0e0bf-81ac-4ad1-8372-f0c01e065005.jpg.webp)**Zoe Kleinman**  
Technology and AI editor

High-profile public service websites like the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) are an attractive target to criminals and hostile regimes for two reasons: a successful hit is likely to cause a lot of chaos, and if money is their aim, the attackers believe the department may pay a ransom to quickly restore its services.

And then of course there's the potential treasure trove of users' data that might be stolen and then used to try to scam individuals further.

But all of this should also mean that the DWP's cyber defences are extremely robust in order to protect it.

It is therefore concerning that in early November Sarah Healey talked about ["extremely old computer systems"](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/c6rrg94lgjrjt?post=asset%3Afb9c5124-dd20-44ee-ac4e-250a1f6f484d#post) at the DWP in a committee hearing.

There's a lot we don't yet know about what's happened this morning and of course it's also possible that some ancient IT infrastructure has gasped its last breath and knocked everything over along with it, but in August a group of 100 tech firms, including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, signed an open letter warning countries and organisations around the world to beef up their cyber defences.

Let's hope the DWP got that memo.

DWP says it has "taken some online services offline as a precaution" which implies that they have possibly seen some kind of activity on their IT network that doesn’t look right.
Taking services offline is part of a "Hail Mary" response we have seen in other cyber incidents, as it kicks the hackers out to prevent further intrusion. Cutting internet connectivity can also help responders preserve evidence, which might help if this is indeed some kind of malicious activity. But we also have to be wary of the language here, as DWP’s actions and wording are reminiscent of the Co-op hack last year.
